name: 5-Amino-1MQ

lead: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), an enzyme that is more active in fat tissue in obesity. It is marketed online as an oral or injectable fat-metabolism supplement.
The evidence is confined to cell and mouse experiments, and no human trials have been published. Its use in looksmaxxing rests on extrapolation from these preclinical results.

paras: Inhibiting NNMT is thought to raise cellular NAD+ levels and the availability of methyl donors, which in mouse adipocytes shifted metabolism towards energy use and reduced fat cell size. In diet-induced obese mice, NNMT inhibitors reduced weight and fat mass, an effect that has not been confirmed in humans.

Human pharmacology, dosing and safety are unknown. The compound is unapproved, sold as a research chemical or supplement of uncertain purity, and its long-term effects on methylation and NAD metabolism have not been evaluated.

lead: 5-Amino-1MQ (5-amino-1-methylquinolinium) is a small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), an enzyme involved in cellular NAD+ and methyl-group metabolism. It carries a permanent positive charge and is therefore handled as a salt, usually the chloride or iodide. Wikipedia notes that it has been sold as a gray-market weight-loss product, sometimes described as a peptide, although it is an experimental small molecule and not a peptide.[1]

Research on it consists of cell and mouse experiments. In a 2018 mouse study, membrane-permeable NNMT inhibitors of this chemical family reversed diet-induced obesity.[2] Wikipedia states that no formal toxicity studies or human clinical trial results exist.[1] The compound is not an approved medicine.
In online communities it is discussed as an oral or injectable fat-loss and metabolism product, an extrapolation from the rodent findings rather than from human data.
infobox: Not approved for medical use; sold as research chemical or supplement [1][3]

paras: 5-Amino-1MQ is a quaternary ammonium compound built on a bicyclic quinolinium core with a methyl group on the ring nitrogen and an amino group at position 5.[3] Because the nitrogen is permanently charged, it is supplied as a salt such as the iodide.[1][3] It is not a peptide, a point Wikipedia emphasises because it is sometimes marketed alongside peptides.[1]

Grokipedia, which is AI-generated and may contain errors, describes the iodide salt as a colored powder soluble in polar solvents and reports a half-maximal inhibitory concentration against NNMT of about 1.2 micromolar from the original characterisation work.[3]

NNMT transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to nicotinamide, producing 1-methylnicotinamide. Its expression is higher in fat tissue in obesity and type 2 diabetes in several reports, which prompted interest in it as a drug target.[4] Inhibiting the enzyme in cultured fat cells is reported to lower 1-methylnicotinamide and raise intracellular NAD+ and related metabolic markers.[3][2]
Researchers hypothesise that this shifts adipocyte metabolism toward energy expenditure and reduces lipid accumulation, although the downstream mechanisms are still under investigation.[2][4]
Human pharmacokinetic data have not been published. Mouse studies used injections of the compound, and published descriptions of the membrane-permeable inhibitors concern rodent tissue exposure.[2]
No studies found in humans. Wikipedia states that the compound has no human clinical trial results and no formal toxicity studies.[1]

Related research (animal): In mice fed a high-fat diet, selective membrane-permeable NNMT inhibitors reduced body weight and white adipose mass, reduced adipocyte size and improved metabolic markers without a change in food intake, according to the 2018 study.[2] A 2021 Scientific Reports study in mice combined NNMT inhibition with a reduced-calorie diet and described a distinct progression of metabolic responses.[5] A review of NNMT in obesity and type 2 diabetes summarises the preclinical and observational literature on the enzyme as a target.[4]

Human safety, interactions and long-term effects are unknown. Because NNMT consumes methyl donors and affects NAD+ metabolism, the consequences of chronic inhibition in people have not been evaluated in published work.[4] The compound is not approved by any regulator and is sold as a research chemical or supplement of unverified purity.[1][3]

The compound is marketed to people seeking fat loss and described as a way to raise NAD+ and metabolic rate. Community use follows supplier and influencer descriptions of the mouse results, and no controlled human outcome data are available to compare with these accounts.[1][3]

lore.intro: The compound circulates in fat-loss supplement and peptide-adjacent marketing as an NAD+ and metabolism booster, with claims derived from mouse data.[1][3]
